mcqs.question: What access-pattern assumption can a time-series storage engine make that a general-purpose database can't?
options: That writes are almost entirely new appends in time order, and reads are almost always scoped by a time window
That every query filters by a unique record ID rather than any range
That data will never be queried again after being written
That all values in the dataset are numeric and never text
mcqs.explanation: The mostly-append, time-ordered write pattern combined with time-range-scoped reads is exactly what lets a time-series engine lay data out and optimize for. Queries aren't ID-lookups, written data is very much queried again, and time-series values aren't restricted to numeric types.

mcqs.question: Why do time-series systems downsample older data into rollups instead of keeping raw resolution forever?
options: Old data becomes legally required to be deleted after downsampling
Rollups let long-range queries scan far fewer, pre-aggregated points instead of scanning and aggregating raw data every time, at the cost of some precision
Raw data corrupts automatically after a certain age
Downsampling is required to make the storage engine's index function at all
mcqs.explanation: Downsampling trades a small amount of precision on old data for a large reduction in storage and query cost, since long-range queries read the small rollups instead of scanning raw history. There's no legal deletion requirement tied to this, no data corruption involved, and the index doesn't depend on downsampling to function.

mcqs.question: A team is building a dedicated observability platform ingesting millions of metric points per second. What does the comparison suggest about using a general-purpose database?
options: A general-purpose database is always the safer, simpler default regardless of ingestion volume
General-purpose databases automatically become time-series databases once ingestion is high enough
A purpose-built TSDB's native rollups and retention policies earn back their operational cost once ingestion volume dominates the system
The choice makes no practical difference for this workload
mcqs.explanation: At the volume described, a purpose-built TSDB's built-in downsampling and retention features are worth their operational overhead — the comparison specifically flags this as the threshold for switching. General-purpose databases don't transform into TSDBs, and the choice has real practical consequences at this scale.

mcqs.question: A metrics system tags every data point with a unique `request_id`. What happens to cardinality as a result?
options: Cardinality stays flat since tags don't affect how series are counted
The metrics system automatically deduplicates request_ids to prevent this
Cardinality only matters for logs, not for metrics
It explodes, since every unique tag combination — including every distinct request_id — creates a new series to store and index
mcqs.explanation: Most time-series systems index every unique tag combination as its own series, so a per-request-unique tag multiplies series count with traffic volume — the core cardinality explosion problem. Tags absolutely affect series count, there's no automatic dedup for this, and cardinality is very much a metrics concern.

mcqs.question: A team wants to tag a latency metric with `user_id` so they can slice performance by user later. What's the better approach per the pitfall?
options: Push high-cardinality identifiers like user_id into logs or traces, and keep the metric's tags limited to naturally bounded dimensions
Add the user_id tag anyway; more tags always add flexibility with no downside
Remove all tags from the metric entirely to avoid any cardinality risk
Store a separate metric per user_id value
mcqs.explanation: High-cardinality identifiers belong in systems built for per-event, high-cardinality data — logs and traces — not in a metric's tag set, which multiplies series count per unique tag combination. Adding the tag anyway risks unbounded cardinality, removing all tags loses useful bounded dimensions too, and a separate metric per user doesn't solve the underlying problem.

mcqs.question: A fleet emitting 600,000 active time series adds a pod_id tag, where pods churn constantly across tens of thousands of identities per day. What happens to series count over a week?
options: Series count only increases by the number of pods running at any single instant
Series count grows by every distinct pod identity ever seen over the week, since each is a new, never-before-indexed tag combination — potentially tens of millions
Series count stays at 600,000 since tags don't affect series identity
The TSDB automatically caps series count at a fixed ceiling regardless of tags
mcqs.explanation: Because cardinality is driven by every distinct tag combination ever recorded, not a snapshot at one instant, constant pod churn accumulates far more unique series than any single moment's pod count would suggest. Series count is directly driven by tag values, and most TSDBs don't impose an automatic hard cap that silently protects against this.
